summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own directed at transgender people, and no Punjab-specific institution dealing with them is recorded. A trans visitor to Punjab therefore stands under India's national framework: Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The underlying national statute is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, receiving presidential assent on 5 December 2019 and in force since 10 January 2020. As enacted it grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

Consensual same-sex acts are no longer criminal in Punjab. On 6 September 2018 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to a self-identified gender identity, and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 codified protection against discrimination. All of these determinations bind Punjab.

Within Punjab the documented signal is institutional rather than criminal. Pride Amritsar cancelled the parade scheduled for 27 April 2025 at the Rose Garden after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition as the reason; the Washington Blade reported the cancellation on 23 April 2025. No state intervention to preserve the event appears in the sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of Punjab's annual public trans assembly.
tangentialFactors:
Opposition to visible trans presence in Punjab is carried by religious bodies rather than by statute. The Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht were named by Pride Amritsar organisers as the resistance that forced the cancellation of the 27 April 2025 parade, and the event did not proceed.

The national framework itself is contested. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the March 2026 amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Judicial protection and legislative retrenchment have moved in opposite directions. The 2018 Navtej Singh Johar ruling and the 2014 NALSA judgment remain binding in Punjab, but the July 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 dropped Section 377 altogether rather than carrying it forward.
localsOnly:
Residents of Punjab can invoke the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 against discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, and the Act's National Council for Transgender Persons is the national body established to oversee its operation. Crimes against transgender people carry imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine.

The Act as passed permits a transgender person to declare a self-perceived gender identity without sex reassignment surgery, drawing on the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment recognising a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity. Whether that declaration route survives for people outside the hijra, kinner and intersex categories after the March 2026 amendment is not resolved in the sources.

Criticism of the Act holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education, so the anti-discrimination guarantee is not backed by a quota entitlement.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Punjab-specific evidence on police conduct, custodial treatment, airport or railway identity checks, or access to transition-related healthcare appears in the sources; assessments of how the national protections are enforced in Punjab remain unresolved rather than established as absent.

The status of the petition against the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act is unresolved after the Supreme Court issued notice on 27 January 2020; no later outcome is sourced.

How the March 2026 amendment is administered in Punjab, including which authorities decide whether an applicant falls within the recognised socio-cultural groups, is not sourced. Nor is the effect of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's omission of Section 377 on non-consensual conduct, since the 2018 judgment had preserved that provision for such acts.
